newsitem.title: LATVIA: Proposed new Latvia finmin backs balanced budget.
newsitem.headline: Proposed new Latvia finmin backs balanced budget.

text.p: Proposed new finance minister Robert Zile said on Wednesday a balanced 1997 budget, a key plank of Latvia's economic policy, was possible due to the current level of revenue collection.

The search for a finance minister has gone on since October and contributed to the downfall of the previous government of Prime Minister Andris Shkele as the premier searched for a candidate to achieve the balanced budget.
"At the moment, meeting a balanced budget seems possible. Information on the state revenue collected up to now does not give any cause for concern," Zile told Reuters in an interview.
The parties in Latvia's eight-party coalition earlier said they backed Zile for the finance post and a vote in parliament is expected on Thursday.
Zile, 38, is from third largest party, Fatherland and Freedom, and is head of the parliamentary budget and finance committee.
The 1997 budget is the first in which the Baltic state has tried to balance the books and comes after a 1996 deficit of 40 million lats. The 1995 deficit was 90 million lats.
Shkele's previous government collapsed after President Guntis Ulmanis called on parliament to reject one of the premier's previous candidates to the finance post.
Shkele resigned in fury but was later recalled to the post and reformed a government earlier this month.
Zile said funds for the budget would decline from 1998 when the government plans to complete privatisation.
Zile said he wanted more long-term planning in tax legislation and was hoping for cooperation from parliament.
"I want to introduce the principle that any new tax legislation comes into force only from the next calendar year or if parliament amends the year's budget," Zile said.
Foreign investors often complain that laws can change overnight in Latvia and call for consistency in legislation.
Zile supported some state regulation of the land market, the development of which is seen as key to the progress of a capital market in Latvia but which is very politicised.
Zile's For Fatherland and Freedom has often spoken out against creating a totally free land market as it believes that foreign investors, mainly Russians, would "buy" Latvia.
"There is no country in the world which has no regulation whatsoever in this sphere," Zile said.
